html:
The ancient trade routes that carried amber, the fossil tree resin of the Baltic and North Sea coasts, south to the Mediterranean. Amber was prized for jewellery and amulets and was called "the gold of the north".

The richest source was the Sambian peninsula, home of the Sambian and other Baltic tribes. Amber moved along rivers such as the Vistula and Oder, through peoples like the Lusatian and Pomeranian cultures, to the Danube and over the Alps to the Adriatic.

Baltic amber lies in the shaft graves of Mycenaean Greece from the 1500s BCE. In Roman times the route ended at Aquileia, whose workshops carved amber for the Roman Empire. Pliny the Elder tells of a knight sent to the Baltic under Nero who came back with a huge load of it. The trade brought southern goods north and gave the Balts a place in the wider world long before written records.
